$comment: ITS-90 thermocouple golden vectors. Voltages marked $quoted are read from the reference tables of NIST Monograph 175, 'Temperature-Electromotive Force Reference Functions and Tables for the Letter-Designated Thermocouple Types Based on the ITS-90' (Burns, Scroger, Strouse, Croarkin, Guthrie; NIST Monograph 175, April 1993), tables 2.3.3 (B), 3.3.3 (R), 4.3.3 (S), 5.3.3 (E), 6.3.3 (J), 7.3.3 (K), 8.3.3 (N) and 9.3.3 (T), all with reference junctions at 0 degrees C. Subrange boundaries and inverse-function error bands marked $quoted are read from the NIST ITS-90 Thermocouple Database (NIST Standard Reference Database 60) file allcoeff.tab. Entries marked $derived are computed by this module from those NIST inputs. Table voltages are in microvolts; engine voltages are in millivolts. DO NOT MODIFY.

directTables.$quoted: NIST Monograph 175 reference tables, thermoelectric voltage E(t90) in microvolts, reference junctions at 0 degrees C.
directTables.$note: toleranceUv covers the rounding of the printed table value. Most tables print to 0.01-0.1 uV; the type J table prints to 1 uV above 760 degrees C, so those points carry their own coarser tolerance.

typeKExponential.$quoted: NIST Monograph 175 table 7.3.1 and allcoeff.tab. Above 0 degrees C the type K reference function is E = sum(c_i t^i) + a0 exp(a1 (t - a2)^2). a0 is stated in the Monograph in microvolts (1.185976E+02 uV = 0.1185976 mV).
typeKExponential.$derived: At t = a2 the exponential contributes exactly a0. At 100 degrees C it contributes about 108.8 uV, so dropping it would report roughly 3987 uV instead of the tabulated 4096.2 uV - a plausible-looking value about 2.7 degrees C low.

inverseSubranges.$quoted: NIST ITS-90 Thermocouple Database (SRD 60), allcoeff.tab, 'coefficients of approximate inverse functions' blocks. Voltage bounds in mV, temperature bounds and error bands in degrees C.

inverseRoundTrip.$derived: Sweep each inverse subrange, take t -> E from the exact reference function, feed E back through the approximate inverse and compare. The residual must land inside the band NIST publishes for that subrange. The inverse is a fit, so exact equality must never be asserted.
inverseRoundTrip.$note: slackC absorbs the finite sweep step and the two-decimal rounding of NIST's published bands.

outOfRange.$derived: Limits restated from the NIST subrange tables above; the engine must refuse rather than extrapolate.
outOfRange.$noteTypeB: 0.29 mV is below type B's inverse floor of 0.291 mV. NIST publishes no inverse below 250 degrees C for type B because E(t) dips negative and doubles back near 21 degrees C, so a voltage there matches two temperatures.

publishedBoundRounding.$derived: NIST prints the inverse voltage bounds rounded to 0.001 mV, so at a type's outer edge the printed bound can sit a fraction of a microvolt inside the reference function's own value at the same temperature. The engine selects on the exact endpoint voltage where it is wider, so a thermocouple at its rated limit is not refused. The gap is always sub-microvolt - if it were larger, the bound would not be a rounding.

coldJunction.$quoted: Both anchor voltages are type K values from NIST Monograph 175 table 7.3.3: E(25 C) = 1000.2 uV, E(300 C) = 12208.6 uV.
coldJunction.$derived: A meter whose cold junction sits at 25 C reads the difference, 12208.6 - 1000.2 = 11208.4 uV. Adding the cold-junction emf back and inverting must return the hot junction, 300 C, within the inverse band plus the rounding of the two quoted table values.
coldJunction.$noteNaive: Reading 11.2084 mV straight off a 0 C table gives 275.80 C; adding the cold-junction temperature to that instead of its voltage lands on 300.80 C, 0.80 C high. Type K is nearly linear over this span, which is exactly why the shortcut survives a bench check and then shows up as a calibration offset. The test asserts the shortcut misses 300 C by more than 0.5 C so the failure mode stays visible.
